title: Ex-CIA officer on UK investigations into alleged Iran, Russia threats
description: NPR's Michel Martin speaks with former CIA senior executive clandestine service officer Daniel Hoffman about investigations in Britain into all
body:
NPR's Michel Martin speaks with former CIA senior executive clandestine service officer Daniel Hoffman about investigations in Britain into alleged threats linked to Iran and Russia.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  We wanted to talk these stories over with someone with experience in intelligence gathering. So we've called Daniel Hoffman. He's a former CIA senior executive clandestine service officer. He's now an advisory board member at the global consulting firm, BGR Group. Good morning, Mr. Hoffman.DANIEL HOFFMAN: Good morning.MARTIN: So let's just talk these through separately. In the case of the charges linked to Iran, we just heard about these alleged operatives carrying out attacks remotely, ranging from this FaceTime call from Iran to coded messages, passed from a New York jail. Is there something that strikes you about these details?HOFFMAN: It does. Look, I think many would like to say that the war - U.S. war against Iran is over, but I would argue that in spite of their depleted military, the Iranians still have the capability to inflict harm on the United States. And for sure, our military bases and other critical locations are in the crosshairs for the Iranians. They want to demonstrate that they have the power to target us kinetically, and I think they believe that would give them leverage in whatever negotiations may or may not take place.MARTIN: You know, the DOJ released a detailed narrative about the accused, including photos of them allegedly planning and directing terrorist attacks. How would they get that information?HOFFMAN: Right. Well, a lot of the information that the terrorists would gain would be through open source. These days, what terrorists like to do is conduct surveillance of targets before they strike. And you can do a lot of that with Google Earth and other tools available on the internet. Now, that's also going to give us an opportunity, if we're watching them, to determine or to learn where they might be planning their next attack.MARTIN: So does that suggest to you that these people were under surveillance at the time, but, oh, some of these attacks did take place? I guess that's one of the things that's sort of confusing about this.HOFFMAN: Right, and there are probably ongoing attacks. So when we make arrests like these, and we hold alleged conspirators in custody, we're also at the same time, in an incident response phase, that there are possible attacks that have been attempted and we need to be aware of that. And we need to conduct sort of a damage assessment to understand where other threats may be out there, and then appropriately defend ourselves. We've seen that already at the U.S. Army bases in the U.K., and Iran has targeted our bases in the Middle East as well. They want to degrade the U.S. ability to project power both in the Middle East and globally.MARTIN: Well, I guess what seems so concerning about this is that these threats seem so dispersed. So the question is, you can't surveil everyone. I guess...HOFFMAN: Right.MARTIN: ...That's the - that is the thing that seems so worrying about this. But these groups seem to operate in these small groups or small cells or individually, all over the world at this point. And I'm just wondering, how does one counter something like that?HOFFMAN: Right. So that's definitely the challenge. These groups are operating reportedly at the behest of Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps. So the goal for the United States has always been to recruit sources inside the institutions of our adversaries, whether it's the KGB during the Cold War, or today in Iran, and that way, we may learn something about their planning. But you're absolutely right - when the attacks are being planned in such a dispersed way, without central control, it makes it extraordinarily difficult for us to detect the threat, way out what we like to call left of boom before any harm is caused to our installations or our homeland and then preempt the threat.MARTIN: OK. Before we let you go, we have a minute left here. Let me talk about that other case, the case of the U.S. soldier arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. I do have to emphasize here, no charges have been filed. A lot we don't know. But what questions do you have about this? What's open in your mind about this?HOFFMAN: Well, look, it's quite significant if he was arrested and on suspicion of espionage, that is assisting a foreign intelligence service, obtaining, disclosing protected information. That's a big deal. We don't know when the Russians have recruited him. We don't know what information he passed. To connect these stories together, I can tell you that Russia and Iran have a very robust intelligence-sharing relationship. And so whatever Russia obtained from this U.S. Army officer, quite possibly, most likely, they passed it to the Iranians, not to mention their other allies. China, for example.MARTIN: OK. I'll just say one more time that individuals are innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. I just think it's important to sort of emphasize that since we do not know. That is former CIA senior executive clandestine service officer Daniel Hoffman. He's now with BGR Group. Mr. Hoffman, thanks so much.HOFFMAN: Thank you.

title: House votes to end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
description: The House was on course for a floor vote Wednesday on whether to impeach Pete Hegseth. That is until House Republicans used a procedural vote t
body:
The House was on course for a floor vote Wednesday on whether to impeach Pete Hegseth. That is until House Republicans used a procedural vote to effectively end the impeachment effort.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:  Critics of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth missed an opportunity to put the House of Representatives on the record.MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  A lone Republican lawmaker, Thomas Massie, sponsored a resolution to impeach Hegseth over the Iran war and other issues. Every other Republican present voted to set the matter aside, and that was just enough in a House that Republicans control for a few more weeks.INSKEEP: NPR Congress reporter Eric McDaniel was at the Capitol and is now here in Studio 31. Eric, thanks for coming by.ERIC MCDANIEL, BYLINE: Of course.INSKEEP: What exactly was that vote yesterday?MCDANIEL: Well, they referred it to committee, right? It was basically a parliamentary maneuver to avoid taking up the impeachment charges and voting on them. Republicans had a simple majority of folks who were actually in attendance at the vote last night, and that was enough to quash it, right? It was the Congress version of making the bill wait on, like, an endless customer support hold.INSKEEP: Or I'm thinking (laughter) - I'm thinking about that old "Schoolhouse Rock!" thing.MCDANIEL: Yeah, yeah. Right.INSKEEP: I'm just a bill. Got stuck in committee. Republicans stood in Trump's corner here - in Hegseth's corner - even after a big election loss that had a lot to do with the war in Iran.MCDANIEL: You know, it's a really good point, and it's something I raised beforehand with a Republican lawmaker. On Monday afternoon, well before the vote, actually, I hopped on the phone with Warren Davidson. He's a Republican congressman from Ohio. And he told me he thinks this war, this conflict, is unconstitutional because it was never authorized by Congress, who, of course, have the power to regulate military conflict. But he doesn't blame Hegseth for that.WARREN DAVIDSON: Trying to scapegoat Pete Hegseth is just a kind of status quo politics in Washington is, oh, we got to find somebody who wasn't on the ballot to take the heat for the way that the election turned out.MCDANIEL: He argues, basically, if Congress has a problem with the war, use the power of the purse and refuse to fund it. He also would like to see the administration articulate a plan.INSKEEP: What about the other charges here involving killing people who'd been on boats in the Caribbean?MCDANIEL: Yeah. You're talking about these boat bombings the administration claims disrupt drug trafficking. There was also a charge for suppressing free speech after the Pentagon tried to punish Mark Kelly - he's a Democratic senator from Arizona - for a video telling service members they are allowed and, in fact, must refuse illegal orders. So a lot of different stuff in there.Hegseth ultimately put out a video last week calling the whole effort a sham. He said, it didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me. Trump also helped to whip votes on this. Here's what the White House said in a statement. Quote  "the administration strongly opposes this impeachment resolution against Secretary Hegseth - a rogue, politically motivated effort to undermine our warfighters, our nation's Constitution and our national security."INSKEEP: Somebody else seems to have helped Hegseth here. Do I understand this correctly? Some Republicans were absent. Democrats actually had enough people physically in Washington, maybe, or at least, you know, on the rolls to pass this, but some were not on the floor for the vote.MCDANIEL: Yeah. I mean, definitely on the rolls, this was always going to be a game of attendance, like we talked about earlier this week...INSKEEP: Yeah.MCDANIEL: ...Once Republicans got their clocks cleaned in the midterms, it was going to be a game to see if they could get themselves back in town. And ultimately, they beat Democrats on attendance performance, as we saw in the vote. Hakeem Jeffries obviously supported this impeachment against Hegseth, so we'll see what happens now.INSKEEP: Although this seems like a lack of seriousness to not show up. What happens now?MCDANIEL: So, next, Steve, these charges aren't going anywhere, but this was always going to face a steep climb. But it was always kind of a messaging effort, too, right? And there are lots of those still to come. The administration asked for an unprecedented $1.5 trillion in defense money. There's also a separate December 11 government funding deadline. There could be new war powers votes, some of which have already attracted - before the midterm elections - Republican support.So still lots of points of leverage left coming for Iran war opponents to extract concessions from the administration, anything from Hegseth's exit to winding down the conflict or, I guess, any number of other things. But what happens next, it isn't going to happen by impeaching or removing the Secretary of Defense. Though that could change when the new Congress is sworn in under Democratic control in January.INSKEEP: NPR's Eric McDaniel. Thanks so much.MCDANIEL: Thank you.

title: Close Trump ally to lead House Republicans next year
description: House Republicans will have a new leader at the start of the new Congress in January: Ohio's Jim Jordan, a co-founder of the ultra-conservative
body:
House Republicans will have a new leader at the start of the new Congress in January: Ohio's Jim Jordan, a co-founder of the ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus and a close ally of President Trump.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:  House Republicans are preparing for life in the minority come January, and they will have a new leader.MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  Yeah. That's Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan. He was selected yesterday as Republicans' top leader in the House after a vote by secret ballot.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JIM JORDAN: When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom, and we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day.MARTIN: Jordan will replace Speaker Mike Johnson, who, after last week's midterm losses, says he is stepping down as the top House Republican.INSKEEP: NPR congressional correspondent Barbara Sprunt is also here in Studio 31. Barbara, thanks for coming by.BARBARA SPRUNT, BYLINE: My pleasure.INSKEEP: OK. So there were two contenders to replace Mike Johnson. One is Jim Jordan. The other is Steve Scalise, who's the No. 2 Republican in the House and has been in or around leadership for many years. What was Jordan's pitch here?SPRUNT: Well, Jordan positioned himself as a fighter. You know, he told his colleagues before the vote that offense, not defense, wins elections. He called himself battle-tested. He's a veteran of the Judiciary and Oversight Committees, two committees that are going to play a very big role in the new Congress. Democrats already have a long list of targets there. And Jordan used that in his pitch to his colleagues, you know, that his leadership experience on both committees would help him navigate those impending investigations.INSKEEP: And apparently enough Republicans agreed with that pitch. So what does that say about the party's expected strategy?SPRUNT: Well, I see this election as sort of a choice between continuity and change. Jordan is certainly the change candidate. He's the co-founder of the ultraconservative Freedom Caucus, which, as we all know, was often a thorn in the side of Republican leadership. Scalise is seen as more of a moderate, an extension of that leadership era of Johnson. And so the vote tells me that House Republicans wanted a clean break from that leadership era. I think folks are craving a new chapter after their massive loss last week.I also think the choice of Jordan is illuminating when you take it alongside the placement of Stephen Miller as the president's new chief of staff. Both have a very combative approach to politics, so much so that I remember former House Speaker John Boehner calling Jordan a legislative terrorist. So the elevation of these two suggests to me that Republicans in the minority are preparing to lean into the fight rather than leaning into compromise.INSKEEP: Just a reminder, the guy calling Jordan a legislative terrorist is himself a Republican.SPRUNT: There we go.INSKEEP: So the guy has sometimes criticized his own party and angered people in his own party. Now, what about the leadership elections in the U.S. Senate?SPRUNT: Well, Senate Republicans held their own closed-door vote yesterday to pick their leaders. There was a small group who wanted to delay the vote, take more time to process the election results. But they ultimately moved ahead with the vote. John Thune, now the majority leader in the Senate, was reelected.INSKEEP: What about on the Democratic side?SPRUNT: Well, there'll be elections next week. The current Democratic leaders are expected to stay in place. That's Hakeem Jeffries in the House, Chuck Schumer in the Senate, both New Yorkers. It's not to say that there aren't some rumblings going on.INSKEEP: Yeah.SPRUNT: No one has come forward to challenge them directly for these top jobs, but there is a group of senators who have said, you know, they want new leadership. That includes Bernie Sanders of Vermont. No surprise there. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan. There are some senator-elects as well, like Annie Andrews of South Carolina, who have said during the campaign they want to see new change.INSKEEP: I wonder if lawmakers are trying to respond to the rumblings of voters who seem unhappy with current leadership, would like to see, in some cases, Schumer go. But Schumer just coordinated a massive election win.SPRUNT: Well, therein lies the tension, right? But I think that speaks to the challenge is that a lot of Democrats feel that they got a message loud and clear from voters, and if they don't respond in a way that reflects that sort of hunger for change in leadership, they feel that they may fall short.INSKEEP: NPR's Barbara Sprunt. Thank you.SPRUNT: You're welcome.

body:
Kennedys sue to block Trump's arch   Descendants of President John F. Kennedy are asking a judge to block President Trump's monumental arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

    
        Politics
    


      
                  
            November 11, 20265:02 AM ET
         
      
   
                              By                
      Linda Kenyon
  
            


      
      KENNEDYS & TRUMP ARCH
    
            
                
                Transcript

                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    




      Descendants of President John F. Kennedy are asking a judge to block President Trump's monumental arch near Arlington National Cemetery.   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:  Nine members of the Kennedy family joined a lawsuit to stop President Trump from building his arch near Arlington National Cemetery. Here's NPR's Linda Kenyon.LINDA KENYON, BYLINE: The Kennedy family members object to the 250-foot arch, arguing it would cast a shadow over the gravesites of their loved ones buried at Arlington National Cemetery. President Trump, as he noted at the White House in December of last year, sees it differently.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: It's something that is so special. It will be like the one in Paris, but to be honest with you, it blows it away.KENYON: But the Democracy Defenders Fund, which represents the Kennedy family, says the arch would be a permanent denigration of the gravesites at Arlington. Attorney Norm Eisen, who represents the fund and the Kennedy family members, says constructing the arch defaces their memories and the memories of all veterans interred at Arlington.NORM EISEN: The Kennedy family members are doing this for themselves, for all of those people and for the rule of law and the separation of powers. Building this arch is illegal.KENYON: The family members in this lawsuit are the children and grandchildren of the late U.S. Senators Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy. The brothers of the slain President John F. Kennedy are buried near the eternal flame that marks his gravesite. Eisen says their descendants are driven by a special cause.EISEN: The veterans and the governments who have already sought to oppose the arch have a very weighty case. But the Kennedy family, in the long tradition of public service that is associated with that name, also wishes to stand up and be heard.KENYON: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who serves as President Trump's Health and Human Services secretary and has a strained relationship with many of his relatives, is not part of the lawsuit.Linda Kenyon, NPR News, Washington.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

      Midterm ballot measures on abortion and transgender issues saw mixed results.   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  Democrats, as you've certainly heard, are bolstered by last week's election results, showing support for their candidates across the country. At the state level, however, they're reviewing mixed opinions on two issues largely backed by Democrats - abortion and transgender rights. Bram Sable-Smith from our partner KFF Health News reports from St. Louis.BRAM SABLE-SMITH, BYLINE: Missouri is often considered a deeply red state. But voters here just rejected an initiative that combined bans on most abortions and on transgender healthcare for minors. Meanwhile, in the state of Washington, often blue in shorthand, voters passed restrictions on trans kids in youth sports. Seems counterintuitive, right? So what to make of these disparate outcomes?SHELBY CHESTNUT: Our research shows that we greatly underestimate red states' ability to show up for bodily autonomy and trans rights, and we overestimate blue states.SABLE-SMITH: Shelby Chestnut's executive director of the National Transgender Law Center. He says years before last week's election, LGBTQ+ advocates in Missouri started going door to door to talk to voters. The sustained organizing was prompted by efforts in 28 states, including Missouri, to pass restrictions on trans healthcare for minors. This year, they're canvassing targeted people who are supportive of abortion access but more ambivalent on trans issues. Chestnut says it paid off.CHESTNUT: And to me, what it says is, we need to build the infrastructure in states, particularly blue states, to defeat these ballot measures.SABLE-SMITH: Experts are also trying to unspool how motivating abortion and trans issues really were in this election. That's a little tricky in Missouri, where the two were explicitly tied together into a single ballot question. But a survey of Missouri voters tried to tease it out, and what they found was that voters on both sides said the most important issue was abortion. But trans issues may not have been what sent people to the polls. In fact, outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters last week he knew Republican candidates were in trouble when he saw they were spending hundreds of millions of dollars on, quote, "transgender ads."(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)RON DESANTIS: That was not the issue motivating voters. And it was kind of like an attempt to just scare Republicans to vote.SABLE-SMITH: While that may have been true for candidates, voters still sent mixed signals on ballot measures around the country. Four states passed restrictions on trans kids in youth sports. Colorado banned gender-affirming surgeries for minors, and Idaho kept its ban on abortion.I'm Bram Sable-Smith.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MARTIN: Bram is with our partner KFF Health News.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results
body:
Swing voters Theresa from Pennsylvania, Jason from North Carolina and Gerald from Georgia. All three voted in this year's midterms and all three have mixed emotions about the results.
                
                    Tara Anand for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tara Anand for NPR
    

   
   Republicans were dealt a stunning rebuke in last week's midterms. But swing voters, who could be decisive in the next election, are more interested in results than investigations or impeachment as Democrats prepare to take power in Congress.   "I am hoping that we don't experience a bunch of gridlock and a lot of whining and crying and just political infighting for the next two years," said Theresa, a voter from Pennsylvania who is participating in NPR's Swing Shift project. "I'm hoping we don't have that. I fear that we will have that."   NPR has agreed not to use the full names of the Swing Shift voters, so they can speak freely about politics without fear of personal or professional repercussions.   
    Loading... 
   Theresa voted for President Biden in 2020, President Trump in 2024 and split her ticket in this year's midterms. Like many voters, her top issue this year was affordability. In a voice memo sent to NPR days after the midterms, Theresa said she is eager for the cost of living to come down.   "I just don't remember it ever being as bad in our time," Theresa said. "And I'm just hoping we get some relief and we get some relief soon."   At 9:56 PM on election night, Wally in Georgia hit send on his voice memo. He had seen enough.   "Just checking in here with a quick note. I'm not surprised at all by the outcome tonight," Wally said. "I believe that this is a lot of Trump's doing and pushback on his style of politics and how he governs."   Wally voted for Trump in 2024 but swung back to Democrats in this year's midterms. He had initially supported Trump in hopes that a Trump presidency would shake up the political system, but that didn't happen and now he says the second Trump term has been exhausting. As he sees it, the decisive Democratic wins signal that the country is ready to move on.    
   "Trump has been shooting himself in the foot for many months now," Wally said. "But voting isn't the end of the game here. We have to hold Democrats to some sort of tangible change and not just promises about what they want to do."   For several of the Swing Shift voters, Tuesday's results came as a surprise.   Jason from North Carolina split his ticket, voting for Democrat Roy Cooper for Senate and the Republican incumbent for the House.   "My congressman was defeated this time by someone that no one's really ever heard of," said Jason, sounding almost puzzled by the blue wave that crashed on North Carolina.   That happened in a lot of places. Jason wants the incoming Democratic Congress to focus on the cost of living and steer clear of impeachment.   "My fear is that the Democrats now are going to spend the next 2 years not focusing on any of the things that they say Trump didn't do," said Jason.   Michelle in Michigan, voted for President Biden in 2020 but chose Republicans in 2024 and again in this year's midterms.   "This is the first time I think ever since I've been voting that not one of the people that I voted for won their election," Michelle said.   Michelle says she understands why so many people voted for Democrats, even if she didn't. Americans are tired, she said, of high gas prices, the cost of living and not being able to afford their groceries. They voted for change.   John from Pennsylvania said it felt like his state went from purple to blue overnight.   "I'm just very surprised," John said. "Not surprised that Democrats had a good night, but they had a very good night. Absolutely amazed that they won in Texas and places that just seemed like they were really red."   He voted for President Biden in 2020 and President Trump in 2024. In the most recent midterms, he stuck with Republicans despite concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.   
   Gerald in Georgia ran through the list of states where Democrats won senate races in disbelief.   "Come on man, Texas turned blue," Gerald said. "South Carolina turned blue, Ohio, Kansas. Like, this was a referendum of epic proportions."   Gerald is a Biden to Trump voter from Georgia, who has gone all in on MAGA. He's already looking ahead to a future without Trump leading Republicans.   "The Donald Trump era for all intents and purposes is coming to an end in 2028 for certain, if not before that," Gerald said.   Before that, though, Democrats will take power in Washington, at least in part.   Swing Shift voters said again and again when asked about their hopes and fears following these midterms that they hope that the incoming Democratic Congress will focus on the issues that impact their daily lives but fear more of the same broken politics.   "I will choose to hope because that's really all we can do is hope," said Michelle. "Hope that the politicians that were voted in will live up to the promises they made and that change will truly be made."   Even though John didn't vote for Democrats this year, he still wants them to tackle the cost of living.   "Over these next 2 years I hope they are concerned with and concentrate on the affordability issue," John said. "I hope they work with President Trump to try to lower prices. I just hope it's not two years of investigations and impeachment hearings."   Anything Democrats pass in a divided government would have to be signed by President Trump. The president has been inconsistent in recent days about whether he wants cooperation or combat with the new Congress.

title: An Iran-backed trio is accused of plotting attacks on a U.K. base hosting U.S. jets
description: A B-1 bomber takes off from RAF Fairford
body:
A B-1 bomber takes off from RAF Fairford in Fairford, England,  Sept. 29, 2026.
                
                    Alastair Grant/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alastair Grant/AP
    

   
   LONDON — Federal prosecutors in New York have charged three men with terrorism offenses over what they describe as an Iran-backed campaign of nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States. The charges include a September plot against a British air base where American forces were stationed.   
   The indictment, unsealed on Tuesday, names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, 32, who holds Iranian and Iraqi citizenship, Mohsen Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, 35, an Iraqi.    Prosecutors allege the men acted on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah to orchestrate, plan and conduct the attacks through a network of associates across Europe and the U.S., targeting Jewish communities and a British base hosting American troops. The indictment cites plots against synagogues in London and in New York. Both Iran's Revolutionary Guard and Kata'ib Hezbollah are designated by the United States as foreign terrorist organizations.   
   The court filings describe an operation that was directed, in part, by the suspects who were thousands of miles away. In April, prosecutors have alleged, the three men gathered in a room and watched an attack unfold live on a large screen via Apple's FaceTime video calling app. Al-Hassani allegedly coached the attacker through igniting and hurling a series of seemingly incendiary devices while Al-Saadi filmed.    The following day, Al-Hassani is accused of guiding another man on a video call as he lit an improvised explosive and threw it at a synagogue in London.   The men "helped orchestrate a campaign of terror" on behalf of the two designated terror groups, according to U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald.   The RAF Fairford plot   The United Kingdom seems to have been a central target of the plot allegedly perpetrated by the three men: among the roughly 18 attacks claimed last spring by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, which prosecutors say was a front for Kata'ib Hezbollah, as many as seven took place in the U.K. It was the most intensely targeted country in Europe, though the indictment does not specify the location of other plots or attacks.   
   These included arson attacks, the use of explosives, and a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London — one of whom was a dual U.S.-British citizen.    Prosecutors say that in April the men sat in a room, and directed an attack remotely, in real time, over FaceTime, telling the attacker when to light and throw what seems to have been some kind of incendiary device.   The next day, one of the men, Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, allegedly told another man attacking a London synagogue to "light it up like a Christmas tree."   According to the indictment, Al-Hassani was operating from Iran, but he began paying associates in Britain in August to film the perimeter of Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford, in Gloucestershire, several hours west of London.    They allegedly obtained vans and drums of fuel, looked into buying chemical accelerants, and gathered metal items that could potentially serve as shrapnel. The vans were fitted with sham branding for a fuel delivery firm as well as a pool supply company.   On Sept. 26, three of these vans had set off toward the base that housed large numbers of U.S. military aircraft. At least two vehicles were stopped at a security roadblock, and British authorities seized all three early the next morning and arrested those inside.   The U.S. almost immediately redeployed several of its long range bombing aircraft from the base at the time of this incident.   The indictment said Al-Saadi had been detained abroad in May and brought to the United States, where prosecutors say he kept directing the network from his jail cell by relaying coded messages through phone calls with relatives in Iraq. He used aliases to refer to his alleged co-conspirators and referred to terrorist activity, including ongoing alleged plots, as "work," while those he spoke to used the phrase "international section" to mean overseas travel, according to the indictment. His sister and mother were among his interlocutors on some of those calls. Three days before the plot, in late September, he allegedly asked them to get money to Al-Hassani for the RAF Fairford operation.   
   British authorities had earlier charged two men with national security related offenses tied to the incident.   U.S. soldier held over Russia allegations   In a separate case, British counterterrorism police said on Tuesday it arrested a 41-year-old member of the U.S. Army on suspicion of offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of Britain's National Security Act 2023.    The suspect, who has not been named by authorities, is a senior U.S. soldier who was stationed at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester, in western England, which is home to NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the U.S. Army's Counterintelligence Command told NPR.   Officers have been searching two addresses in the same region of Gloucestershire, to the west of London. The man is being held at a London police station. Police said the allegations concern Russia, and the investigation was "very much ongoing," according to Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing in the U.K.   FBI Director Kash Patel called the arrest important in the context of an uptick in FBI counterintelligence arrest, and said it "involves allegations of espionage" — without giving further details.   "The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent," Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in a statement to NPR.   The U.S. footprint in Britain   Though unrelated, both these cases have occurred in the U.K., a country which hosts a large American military presence. At the start of the war in Iran, Britain's Defense Ministry confirmed to the U.K. Parliament in March that U.S. forces operate eleven RAF bases across the country, with approximately 12,300 American military and civilian defense personnel at various sites.    Responding in January to a written question from a member of Parliament, the ministry said that there were around 11,000 uniformed U.S. personnel in the country, excluding families, civilians and contractors.    
   The ministry has declined to give figures for individual bases, citing the security of personnel.   The U.S. Air Force's two main operating bases are RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, in eastern England. Other sites include RAF Croughton, a communications station in Northamptonshire, and RAF Menwith Hill in North Yorkshire, used primarily by the National Security Agency, according to a House of Commons Library briefing. RAF Fairford serves as a forward operating base for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command.   In March, the British government allowed the U.S. to use British bases for limited strikes against missile sites in Iran, according to a parliamentary research service, which identifies Fairford as one of the bases potentially involved.   The threat picture around some U.S. bases seems to have sharpened in recent days. The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that the U.S. military had moved aircraft out of RAF Mildenhall on Monday because of a threat from Iran. NPR did not independently confirm the reports.   Neither the U.K. nor the U.S. government has confirmed the reason for the aircraft movements that have been reported. Britain's Defense Ministry has said aircraft relocate routinely for operational reasons.

title: House effectively ends Hegseth impeachment. And, 3 men accused of plotting U.K. attacks
description: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for
body:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   The House has effectively killed Republican Rep. Thomas Massie's effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The chamber voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment articles back to the House Judiciary Committee for review. The move circumvents any potential floor vote on the impeachment and virtually ensures it won't be addressed before the current Congress session ends. Massie had reintroduced the impeachment articles on Monday, accusing Hegseth of high crimes related to the war with Iran and U.S. strikes against drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon on Nov. 10, 2026.
                
                    Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 NPR's Eric McDaniel describes yesterday's vote to Up First as a game of attendance. There were enough Democrats in Washington to pass the impeachment resolution, but not enough were on the floor to vote, so Republicans had the simple majority. McDaniel spoke to Warren Davidson, a GOP congressman from Ohio, the day before the vote. Davidson said he thinks the war in Iran is unconstitutional, but argued that Hegseth was just a scapegoat for the "status quo politics in Washington."➡️ The GOP had a lot on their agenda yesterday. The Republican-controlled House Oversight Committee released a report on its investigation into the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associates. The report concluded that the federal government mishandled criminal investigations into the disgraced financier and failed survivors.   
   Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio will be the new minority leader of the House. House Republicans voted yesterday to replace Speaker Mike Johnson, who is stepping down after last week's midterm losses. At 62, Jordan brings experience from the House Oversight and Judiciary committees. The two panels are poised to play a central role in the new Congress as Democrats plan investigations into President Trump and his administration.   🎧 NPR's Barbara Sprunt says she viewed the election as a choice between continuity and change, and Jordan clearly represented change. Jordan's selection, along with Stephen Miller's appointment as the president's new chief of staff, highlights a shift towards a combative political approach, Sprunt says. Democratic leadership elections are expected to happen next week and are likely to keep current leaders Hakeem Jeffries in the House and Chuck Schumer in the Senate in place.   U.S. federal prosecutors have indicted three men accused of being Iran-backed operatives allegedly involved in nearly 20 terrorist attacks and attempted attacks in Europe and the U.S. The charges include a plot in September against a British air base where American forces were stationed. The Justice Department says some of these attacks were directed live via FaceTime from Iraq.   
   🎧 Federal prosecutors in Manhattan accuse the men of working for Iran's Revolutionary Guard and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah, both classified as terrorist groups, according to reporter Willem Marx. Seven of the attacks happened in Britain. They included arson, explosives and a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London. Marx also noted that, in a separate case, British counter-terrorism police have arrested a 41-year-old U.S. Army soldier on suspicion of spying for Russia under the National Security Act. Authorities emphasized that this spying investigation is not linked to the Iran-related case. But Marx says these incidents raise significant concerns about security around American military bases in Britain and the safety of nearby residents.Veterans in the new Congress   by Quil Lawrence, Veterans correspondent   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Virginia Democratic Congressional candidate Elaine Luria arrives to deliver remarks during an election night watch party at Holiday Inn Virginia Beach on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Virginia Beach, Virginia. Luria faces incumbent Rep. Jen Kiggans (R-VA) in a rematch after losing to her in Virginia's 2nd District in 2022.
                
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Finn Gomez/Getty Images
    

   
   A Navy admiral fired by the Trump administration is returning to Washington as a Democratic congresswoman. In Virginia, a former Army Colonel beat another former Army Colonel, and a female Navy vet won a rematch to unseat another female Navy vet. In Florida, a staunchly pro-Trump Air Force Vet narrowly fended off a former Army Brigadier General (both also women.) In Montana, two military veterans lost, splitting the votes against a Republican former attorney general with no military background.   What conclusion to draw? There isn't any!   Americans dependably say they admire military service, and political campaigns recruit vets to run on tough races. Whether it works remains an open question, though some research suggests Democrats in particular may benefit from veterans status with voters.   The next Congress includes at least 80 veterans, with a few races still too close to call. And according to With Honor, which supports veteran candidates from both parties who promise to sponsor legislation across the aisle, more than 50 vets in the next Congress have signed their pledge.   But the number of vets is shrinking, down to 15% from the 19% currently in office. That's probably just demographics. Relatively few Americans serve in today's all-volunteer military, while past generations were drafted by the millions to Vietnam and Korea. During World War 2, military service was almost a given for men. When that generation entered politics, both chambers had around 70% veterans for a decade, from 1965 to 1975.   
   The 120th Congress will host more female vets than ever, about double the last class. Analysis by the Veterans Campaign and the University of San Francisco found that Democrats chose veterans as candidates for the toughest races, in districts President Trump won in 2024 by an average of 22 points.   There's another way vets are serving: as poll workers. The group Vet the Vote recruits veterans and their families to help run elections. Starting from a goal of 150,000 volunteers during the 2024 presidential cycle, their campaign counted more than 175,000 for this midterm, from all 50 states, helping bolster the understaffed and overworked polling officials nationwide. The group says it had volunteers in 4 out of 5 zip codes across the country.   And veterans like to vote. Syracuse University D'Aniello Institute for Veterans and Military Families found that vets turned out in relatively higher numbers than civilians in every election since 2014, a difference especially pronounced in midterm elections.   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                In this image, you can see that moment of pause: sometimes the hardest part about talking to other people isn't finding the right words to say, but deciding if you should say anything at all.
                
                    Abi Inman/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Abi Inman/NPR
    

   
   Being honest with people can be tricky. Sometimes, deciding whether to say anything at all can be harder than finding the right words to say. Social psychologist Vanessa Bohns says that giving feedback or criticism often feels like a dilemma. But with care, you can make better choices about when to share your thoughts. Bohns has shared three questions with Life Kit that you could consider before voicing your opinion.   🗣️ Is this information helpful? Honesty is beneficial if your feedback helps someone improve, avoid embarrassment or learn something about themselves. If your comments are mean-spirited, irrelevant or impractical to enact, it's probably better to stay silent.🗣️ Would I want to hear this? Just because you don't want to share the truth doesn't mean the other person doesn't want to hear it. A 2022 survey found that people often underestimate others' desire for feedback even when it is constructive.🗣️ Do they want your feedback? When in doubt, don't assume you know what someone needs. Pre-assessing how valuable your advice is or how well someone can handle the truth can make well-meaning feedback sound patronizing.   
   For more guidance on how to share good and bad news, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                After playing and singing "Little Wonders," by Rob Thomas for Army veteran John Fay at the DC VA Medical Center's Hospice Unit, Musicians On Call performer, Dante Ciolfi, thanks Fay for his service.
                
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
    

   
   Volunteer musicians from Musicians On Call perform for veterans at the VA Medical Center in Washington, D.C., and other hospitalized patients nationwide. They typically visit hospitals three to four times a month.The Rembrandt House Museum in Amsterdam came alive recently as a renowned tattoo artist brought 17th-century masterpieces to life on visitors' skin.The Professional Women's Hockey League has announced the name of its new women's hockey team: the San José Sea Lions. (via KQED)   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: Kennedy relatives join the fight against Trump's arch, alleging harm to JFK's grave
description: The gravesite of former President John F
body:
The gravesite of former President John F. Kennedy at Arlington National Cemetery sits on the same axis as the Lincoln Memorial (seen in the distance). Kennedy's ancestors say Trump's 250-foot arch would not only disrupt the view between the monuments, but cast a shadow over his grave.
                
                    Jewel Samad/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jewel Samad/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   One of America's most prominent political dynasties has waded into the growing fight against President Trump's proposed arch in Washington, D.C.   Nine members of the Kennedy family filed suit in federal court on Tuesday to block the 250-foot structure, saying it would obstruct their relatives' gravesites — including the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame — at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.   "A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come," Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said in a statement on behalf of the family.   
   The plaintiffs include children of Sen. Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy and a son of Sen. Edward M. Kennedy, all three of whom are buried at Arlington National Cemetery. There is one noticeable absence: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., did not join his siblings in the lawsuit against his own administration.   "It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in a statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."   The Kennedys' motion, filed hours before Veterans' Day, adds a highly personal layer to the ongoing legal fight.   "[The arch] constitutes nothing less than a permanent denigration of the Kennedy Gravesites and the final resting place for Plaintiffs' parents and grandparents," they wrote in their 27-page filing. "Plaintiffs would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended."   The Kennedys seek to join the existing federal lawsuit against the arch, which combines two cases: one brought by Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian earlier this year, and another filed by the governments of D.C. and Virginia late last month. The Arlington County Board has also filed a lawsuit in Virginia.   
    Loading... 
   The Trump administration has raced its arch through the federal approvals process over the past year, culminating in a final green light from the National Capital Planning Commission on Thursday. Officials had previously said they could break ground in Memorial Circle that same day.   But within moments of the late-night approval, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan stepped in with an order blocking construction for two weeks while she evaluates the broader legal challenges.   
   One of the main arguments against the arch is that its construction is unlawful without congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. The administration maintains that the arch is justified by a century-old authorization of two never-built columns at that same location, which did not seem to convince the judge: Chutkan wrote last week that "merely to state this argument is to reveal its flaws."   The administration has also argued that the case should be thrown out because of plaintiffs' lack of standing, which was the Supreme Court's reasoning in the White House ballroom case. But Chutkan has said D.C. and Virginia likely have standing to sue over the arch, given the financial and logistical harms they would suffer.   David Super, a Georgetown University law professor, told NPR in an email that he believes the Kennedys' involvement only strengthens the plaintiffs' standing.   "I can imagine ... that a judge on any level would feel uncomfortable denigrating their concerns over their family graves the way the Supreme Court denigrated the plaintiffs' interest in the White House ballroom case," he wrote. "And coming at a time when the Administration is hinting that it might tear down the Kennedy Center, this certainly makes the President look insensitive or even hostile to his revered predecessor."   Several Kennedy family members have spoken out against Trump's attempted takeover of the Kennedy Center, which is the subject of a separate lawsuit.   
   Arlington National Cemetery is central to the arch fight     
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                JFK's gravesite, featuring an eternal flame, sits just below Arlington House, the former home of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee. Trump's arch would stand in a traffic circle on the bridge that connects Arlington House to D.C.'s National Mall.
                
                    Brendan Smialowksi/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Brendan Smialowksi/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The cemetery says JFK's gravesite is one of its two most-visited locations, along with the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.   The Kennedys explain in their legal filing that JFK's family chose Arlington as his final resting place so that his gravesite could be accessible to the public.   
   "President Kennedy himself visited the Cemetery and stood where he is now buried," they wrote. "The vista looking back toward the District from the spot where his grave now stands was one of his favorites. While looking out, he remarked, 'I could stay here forever.'"   The grave was intentionally placed on the same axis as the bridge connecting Arlington House (the former home of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee) to the Lincoln Memorial, with Kennedy's personal secretary remarking that he was "the link between Lincoln and Lee."   Kennedy's gravesite is topped with an eternal flame, which has burned since his funeral in November 1963. The Kennedys said their ancestors were "assured that all aspects of the design would safeguard visibility of the Eternal Flame" from the bridge, even with its intentionally low profile to preserve views of Arlington House.   The arch, they say, would block those views. The Trump administration has acknowledged that the arch would disrupt the historic significance of many nearby memorials, but has said building it anywhere else would defeat its purpose.   The Kennedy complaint goes a step further, citing a recent forensic analysis by the Washington Post that shows the arch would cast shadows over tens of thousands of graves. It would darken JFK's memorial on 50 days of the year, and briefly block the eternal flame on almost half of those.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The Kennedy family members included this photo in their legal filing, showing the eternal flame at JFK's gravesite on the night of his funeral in November 1963.
                
                    Abbie Rowe. White House Photographs. John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, Boston
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Abbie Rowe. White House Photographs. John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, Boston
    

   
   The Trump administration has said the arch will be topped with its own eternal flame, per the controversial lighting recommendations of the Federal Aviation Administration.   
   The Kennedys said they often visit their family's graves in the morning for extra privacy — exactly the time of day that the Post analysis found the shadows would be most pronounced.   "Plaintiffs' visits to these would literally be shadowed by the Arch, an unlawfully-created structure," the filing reads. "The shadow the Arch would leave over the Kennedy Gravesites would fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the Gravesites."   Arlington National Cemetery is the final resting place for more than 400,000 service members, veterans and their relatives.   
   The White House has characterized the arch as a tribute to the nation's military heritage, saying it will "enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike."   But many of those veterans and their family members have spoken out vehemently against the arch: at protests in Memorial Circle, in tens of thousands of written comments as part of the federal review process, over nearly nine impassioned hours of public testimony during last Thursday's planning commission meeting.   Critics say the arch would disrespect those buried at Arlington and disrupt the solemnity of the space for the loved ones who visit them. They say construction — which the Trump administration estimates would involve 20-hour days — would interfere with the 24 to 27 funeral services held there every weekday.   Veterans have said that if Trump — who got five draft deferments during the Vietnam War — really wants to honor their service, he would stop cutting resources for them.   A flurry of court filings argue for a more permanent ban on the arch    The Trump administration has also recast the arch as a military structure (on a public-facing website and in recent court filings), though the plan that received final approval last week has no details about national security. The judge did not seem to find that late-stage argument compelling in her order last week.   
   In a 10-page declaration filed Tuesday, a retired military general argued that the arch would actually endanger national security.   
   Ret. U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Steven Anderson warned that storing ammunition in a tourist attraction would constitute a "tremendous risk," and that launching drones in that area — especially so close to D.C.'s airport — "poses clear hazards" to civilians.   "Not only is the Arch not suitable for any practical military facility, but it actually degrades security in the National Capital Region by placing a high-payoff target for our enemies just a few meters from a major road network and the traffic circle that surrounds the Arch," Anderson wrote.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Protestors rally beneath a miniature mock-up of the arch during a demonstration at Memorial Circle last Thursday. The administration wants the real version to be 250 feet tall, topped with gold statues and an eternal flame.
                
                    Tom Brenner/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner/Getty Images
    

   
   He pointed to bombings in Beirut in 1983 and Oklahoma in 1995 as "two examples of the danger posed by allowing vehicles within close proximity of comparable military or law enforcement targets."   Anderson's declaration was part of a slew of documents that the veterans filed this week in their quest for a more permanent ban on the arch.   Democrats have also vowed to use their forthcoming majority in Congress to block Trump's construction projects and investigate potential wrongdoing.   But experts told NPR earlier this week that given Trump's veto power, Congress is better positioned to tackle that fight through oversight hearings and funding restrictions. The future of the arch, they say, will likely be up to the Supreme Court.

schema.headline: Kennedy relatives join the fight against Trump's arch, alleging harm to JFK's grave
